title: What is PMS vs PMDD and how do you know the difference
content:
Title:

What is PMS vs PMDD, and how do you know the difference?

Keywords:

premenstrual syndrome, PMS, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, PMDD, menstrual cycle, mood swings, irritability, bloating, breast tenderness, fatigue, cravings, emotional symptoms, mental health, anxiety, depression,

Short Description:

PMS and PMDD are often confused, but one is far more serious than the other. Learn how to tell the difference, track your symptoms, and know when it’s time to see a doctor.

What is PMS vs PMDD, and how do you know the difference?

Every month, many women go through physical and emotional changes before their period. For some, it’s mild breast tenderness, tiredness, or feeling easily irritated.

But for others, it’s much heavier. They feel deeply sad, angry, anxious, or even hopeless, and it keeps happening.

In Nigeria, these symptoms are often misunderstood. You’ll hear things like “Is it not just period?” or “You too dey do like say you wan die because of small blood wey dey comot for your bosy.” But sometimes, it’s not ordinary at all.

There is a difference between PMS and PMDD, and knowing where you fall can change how you take care of yourself.

Let’s take a look at what PMS and PMDD are, how to tell them apart, and when it’s time to seek help.

What Is PMS (Premenstrual Syndrome)?

PMS is the collection of physical and emotional symptoms many women experience in the 1–2 weeks before their period starts. It’s incredibly common; studies show that up to 90% of women experience some form of PMS during their reproductive years.

Typical symptoms include:

  • Bloating or weight gain
  • Breast tenderness
  • Headaches or body aches
  • Mood swings, irritability, or crying easily
  • Fatigue or trouble sleeping
  • Food cravings, especially for sweets or salty snacks

For most women, these symptoms are uncomfortable but manageable. They usually ease once menstruation begins and don’t interfere too much with day-to-day life.

However, when these symptoms start affecting your ability to concentrate, maintain relationships, or function normally, it may point to something more than PMS.

What is PMDD (Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder)?

PMDD is a much more severe form of PMS. It’s not just mood swings or tiredness; it feels like a serious emotional breakdown that shows up every month before your period.

Women with PMDD often experience:

  • Deep sadness or depression
  • Sudden anger or outbursts
  • Anxiety or panic attacks
  • Feeling hopeless or worthless
  • Losing interest in things they normally enjoy
  • Trouble focusing
  • Thoughts of self-harm or suicide

It can feel like you’re a different person entirely before your period. Then, once the period starts, the symptoms disappear until next month.

PMDD affects about 3 to 8% of menstruating women. It’s not something you can “snap out of” or pray away. It’s a real medical condition and is recognised as a mental health disorder.

Key Differences at a Glance

PMS and PMDD may happen around the same time in your cycle, but the severity, emotional impact, and life disruption are what set them apart.

How to Know Which One You Have

The key difference lies in how much your symptoms affect your daily life.

If you feel uncomfortable but can still function, it’s likely PMS. But if your emotions feel overwhelming, and your work, relationships, or mental health suffer every month, PMDD may be the cause.

To know for sure, track your symptoms daily for at least two cycles. Note when they start, how severe they are, and when they ease.

Treatment Options That Work

Let’s take a look at what could help manage each condition in more detail.

For PMS

  • Exercise regularly
  • Reduce sugar, caffeine, and alcohol
  • Use pain relief (e.g., paracetamol, ibuprofen)
  • Try supplements like calcium, magnesium, or vitamin B6

For PMDD

  • Antidepressants (SSRIs): help balance mood
  • Hormonal birth control: to stabilise hormones
  • CBT (therapy): to manage emotional symptoms
  • In severe cases, hormone-blocking injections may be used

Herbal remedies can help some women, but don’t rely on them alone. Always speak to a doctor

Next Steps

If your pre-period symptoms are so bad that you cry uncontrollably, lash out at people you care about, or feel like disappearing every month, that’s not just regular PMS. It could be PMDD, and it deserves real attention.

Please see a doctor if:

  • You feel hopeless, angry, or overwhelmed before your period
  • Your symptoms are ruining your relationships or work life
  • You’ve had thoughts of harming yourself
  • Nothing you’ve tried is helping

You’re not weak. You’re not “too emotional.” And you’re definitely not alone. Getting the right help can change everything.

I’ve said my part. Now I want to hear yours: what does PMS or PMDD look like in your life?

title: What Really Is HPV
content:
Title: What Really Is HPV?

Keywords: HPV, human papillomavirus, HPV symptoms, HPV prevention, HPV transmission, HPV testing, HPV vaccine, cervical cancer, genital warts, HPV risks

Short Description:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is the world's most common sexually transmitted infection, yet many people still misunderstand it. This guide breaks down what HPV is, how it spreads, the health problems it can cause, and the most effective ways to prevent it.

What Really Is HPV?

Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is the most common sexually transmitted infection in the world, affecting both men and women.

In fact, most sexually active people will contract HPV at some point in their lives.

While many HPV infections clear up on their own, certain strains can cause serious health problems like cervical cancer, other genital cancers, and genital warts.

The good news is that HPV is largely preventable through vaccination, safe sexual practices, and regular screening.

Understanding the virus is the first step to protecting yourself and your loved ones.

What is HPV?

HPV stands for Human Papillomavirus, but it's not just one virus. It's a large group of more than 200 related viruses, each with its own number (or "type").

HPV types are grouped into two main categories:

Low-risk HPV

  • It can cause skin or genital warts.
  • Does not cause cancer.
  • Examples: HPV types 6 and 11 (responsible for about 90% of genital wart cases).

High-risk HPV

  • It can cause abnormal cell changes that may develop into cancer if left untreated.
  • Examples: HPV types 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers worldwide (IARC).
  • Linked to cancers of the cervix, anus, penis, vulva, vagina, and throat.

HPV infects the skin and mucous membranes (the moist surfaces inside the body). Because it can hide without showing symptoms, many people unknowingly spread it while infected.

How HPV Spreads

HPV is primarily passed through intimate skin-to-skin contact, and it's surprisingly easy to transmit even if no symptoms are visible.

  • Vaginal and anal sex are the most common routes of transmission.
  • Oral sex also spreads HPV, contributing to infections in the mouth and throat.
  • Genital contact without penetration, like skin rubbing or manual stimulation, can spread the virus too.
  • Even asymptomatic individuals can spread HPV, because they often don't know they're infected.
  • In rare cases, HPV can be passed from a pregnant woman to her baby during childbirth, leading to respiratory issues in the newborn.

HPV spreads easily through close, intimacy-based contact, even when you don't see any signs. Using protection helps, but it doesn't eliminate risk completely, because the virus can still infect areas not covered.

Symptoms of HPV

Most people with HPV never develop symptoms and may not even know they are infected. This is why the virus can spread so easily; it often remains silent.

When symptoms do appear, they depend on the type of HPV:

  • Low-risk types: May cause genital warts, small growths, or lumps that can appear on the vulva, vagina, cervix, penis, scrotum, anus, or groin. These warts can be raised, flat, single, multiple, or cauliflower-shaped
  • High-risk types: Usually cause no visible symptoms until more serious conditions develop, such as precancerous changes or cancer in the cervix, anus, throat, or genitals.

It's important to remember that the absence of symptoms does not mean the absence of infection. Regular screening is the only way to detect high-risk HPV early.

Health Problems Caused by HPV

HPV can lead to a range of conditions, depending on the strain. While many infections clear without harm, persistent infection with certain types can cause severe disease.

Common health issues linked to HPV include:

  • Cervical cancer: Almost all cervical cancer cases are caused by high-risk HPV types.
  • Other genital cancers: Vaginal, vulvar, penile, and anal cancers are also linked to persistent infection.
  • Oropharyngeal cancer: Cancer at the back of the throat, base of the tongue, or tonsils.
  • Genital warts: Caused by low-risk HPV types; not life-threatening but can cause discomfort and emotional distress.
  • Respiratory papillomatosis: A rare condition where warts grow inside the airways, including the voice box and windpipe, potentially causing breathing or speech problems.

HPV-related cancers often develop years after the initial infection, which is why prevention and early detection are crucial.

Who Is at Risk?

Anyone who is sexually active can get HPV, regardless of age, gender, or sexual orientation. The virus is so prevalent that most people will contract it at some point in their lives.

Factors that can increase the risk include:

  • Having multiple sexual partners.
  • Starting sexual activity at a young age.
  • Having a partner who has had numerous partners.
  • Weakened immune system (e.g., from HIV infection or certain medications).
  • Not receiving the HPV vaccine.
  • History of other sexually transmitted diseases.

It's important to remember that even one sexual partner is enough to contract HPV if they carry the virus.

Prevention

While HPV is common, there are effective ways to protect yourself and reduce the risk of infection:

  • HPV vaccination: Safe and highly effective at preventing infection from the most dangerous HPV types. Best given before the start of sexual activity, but can still benefit those already sexually active.
  • Regular cervical screening: Pap smears and/or HPV tests help detect early changes in cervical cells before they turn into cancer.
  • Practice safer sex: Using condoms and dental dams reduces the risk, although it doesn't eliminate it.
  • Limit sexual partners: Reducing the number of sexual partners lowers your exposure risk.
  • Boost immunity: Maintaining a healthy lifestyle supports the body's ability to clear HPV naturally.

Testing and Treatment

There is no general test for all HPV types, and most people never know they have the virus unless it causes health problems.

Testing

  • Cervical screening (Pap smear and/or HPV test): Checks for high-risk HPV and abnormal cell changes in the cervix.
  • No routine HPV test for men: Diagnosis in men is usually based on visible symptoms like genital warts or related cancers.
  • Follow-up procedures: If abnormal cells are found, further tests, such as colposcopy or biopsy, may be performed.

Treatment

  • No cure for HPV itself: In most cases, the body's immune system clears the infection naturally.

Treating related conditions:

  • Genital warts can be removed with prescription creams, freezing, or minor surgery.
  • Precancerous cell changes can be treated before they develop into cancer.
  • Cancers caused by HPV are treated with surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation, depending on the stage.

Regular check-ups and early treatment of abnormalities are key to preventing serious complications.

Final Takeaway

Silence around HPV has allowed myths and fear to thrive.

The more we speak openly about it, the easier it becomes for others to learn about it, get tested, and protect themselves.

Your personal experience, whether it's about prevention, diagnosis, or recovery, could be the exact insight someone else has been searching for.

Let's make this a conversation people aren't afraid to have.

Researched by Victoria Odueso

title: Why do women get gestational diabetes
content:
Title: Why Do Women Get Gestational Diabetes?

Keywords: gestational diabetes, pregnancy, blood sugar, insulin resistance, hormones, placenta, overweight, family history, older age, large baby, PCOS, multiple pregnancy, lifestyle

Short Description:
Gestational diabetes happens when pregnancy hormones affect how the body uses insulin, causing blood sugar levels to rise. This article looks at the leading causes, risk factors, and other factors that can increase a woman's chances during pregnancy.

Why do women get gestational diabetes?

Gestational diabetes is a type of diabetes that develops during pregnancy. It occurs when the body cannot properly use insulin, leading to high blood sugar levels.

This condition is important because it affects both the mother and the baby if not well managed.

Many women do not notice symptoms, which is why doctors screen for them during routine antenatal care.

In this article, we'll look at what this condition means for an expecting mother.

What Causes Gestational Diabetes?

During pregnancy, the body produces hormones that support the baby's growth. But some of these hormones also reduce insulin's effectiveness.

When insulin becomes less effective, sugar builds up in the blood, and that's when gestational diabetes can develop.

Some key reasons are:

  • Hormonal changes: Hormones such as human placental lactogen, estrogen, cortisol, and progesterone increase insulin resistance.
  • Insulin resistance: The body needs more insulin to keep blood sugar normal, but sometimes it cannot make enough.
  • Placental growth: As pregnancy progresses and the placenta grows, hormone levels rise further, increasing the risk later in pregnancy.

Who Is at Higher Risk?

Not every pregnant woman will develop gestational diabetes, but some are more likely to get it than others. The major risk factors include:

  • Being overweight before pregnancy: Women who are overweight or obese have a higher chance.
  • Family history of diabetes: If your parents or siblings have diabetes, your risk is higher.
  • Older age: Women aged 30–35 years have a greater risk than younger mothers.
  • Previous pregnancy history: If you had gestational diabetes before, or gave birth to a very big baby (more than 4 kg), your chances increase.
  • Ethnic background: Studies show that African women tend to have higher rates of gestational diabetes compared to women in some other parts of the world.

Other Contributing Factors

Apart from weight, age, and family history, some other things can make a woman more likely to have gestational diabetes:

  • Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): Women with PCOS often have insulin resistance, which makes them more prone to diabetes in pregnancy.
  • Lifestyle factors: Eating a lot of processed foods, frequent consumption of sugary drinks, and a lack of regular exercise increase the risk. These habits are becoming more common in many cities, where many women are less physically active, and rates of overweight are rising.
  • Multiple pregnancy: Carrying twins or triplets can lead to higher hormone levels, which can raise blood sugar.

What Happens if Gestational Diabetes Is Left Unmanaged?

When gestational diabetes is not properly managed, it can affect both mother and baby. The risks may not be apparent immediately, but can have serious short- and long-term consequences.

For the mother:

  • High blood pressure & preeclampsia: GDM increases the risk of pregnancy-induced hypertension, which can progress to preeclampsia, a dangerous condition that threatens both mother and baby.
  • Delivery complications: Higher chance of needing a cesarean section (C-section) due to a large baby size.
  • Future diabetes: Women with GDM have a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes later in life.

For the baby:

  • Macrosomia (large baby): Excess sugar from the mother crosses the placenta, making the baby grow bigger than normal, which can cause birth injuries during delivery.
  • Preterm birth: High blood sugar may trigger early labor or require early delivery for safety.
  • Low blood sugar after birth (neonatal hypoglycemia): Babies may struggle to maintain normal blood sugar once the umbilical cord is cut.
  • Breathing difficulties: Babies born early may develop respiratory distress syndrome.
  • Future risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes: Children of mothers with untreated GDM are more likely to face these issues later in life.

Untreated gestational diabetes affects two lives at once. Proper screening, healthy lifestyle choices, and medical care can drastically reduce these risks.

Conclusion

Gestational diabetes is a condition every pregnant woman should know about, especially because it often shows no signs until tests are done. Staying informed makes it easier to protect both mother and baby during pregnancy.

What are your thoughts?

Have you or someone you know ever been screened for gestational diabetes during pregnancy? I'd love to hear your experience in the comments.

title: Why Women Get Migraines More Often
content:
Title:
Why Women Get Migraines More Often
Keywords:
migraine, women, hormones, estrogen, menstrual migraine, perimenopause, pregnancy,
triggers, stress, headache, migraine management, neuro-hormonal
Short Description:
Migraines affect women more than men, often linked to hormonal changes and daily triggers.
This article explores why migraines are more common in women and provides tips to reduce
attacks.






























Why Women Get Migraines More Often
Migraines affect women far more than men, and the numbers make that clear.
According to data published, the global prevalence of migraine is 20.7% in women compared to
9.7% in men. In simple terms, women are about twice as likely to experience migraines as men.
For many women, these migraines don’t appear out of nowhere.
They often show up around menstruation, during pregnancy, after childbirth, or as menopause
approaches. This pattern leaves a lot of women asking the same question: Why does this keep
happening at certain stages of my life?
To answer that, we need to look closely at what’s happening inside the female body, especially
the role of hormones.
How Hormones Play a Big Role in Migraines
The biggest reason women get migraines more often than men is hormonal changes, especially
changes in a hormone called estrogen.
Estrogen affects how the brain handles pain. When estrogen levels are steady, the brain is
usually calmer. But when estrogen drops suddenly, it can trigger a migraine attack.
This is why migraines in women often follow a pattern.
Here’s how hormones come into play:
● Before or during menstruation: Estrogen levels drop sharply just before a period,
which can trigger migraines in many women. (This is often called menstrual migraine)
● During pregnancy: Estrogen stays high and stable for months. Many women notice
their migraines improve during this time.
● After childbirth: Estrogen drops quickly after delivery, and migraines may return or
become worse.
● Perimenopause: Hormone levels rise and fall unpredictably, which can increase
migraine attacks.
● After menopause: Once hormones settle at a lower level, migraines often reduce for
many women.
Research consistently shows this link between estrogen changes and migraines in women.
So, migraines in women are not random or “in the head.” They are often the brain’s response to
hormonal shifts happening in the body.


What’s Happening Inside the Brain During a Migraine
A migraine is not just pain.
It starts in the brain, and women’s brains may be more sensitive to migraine triggers, especially
when hormones are changing.
One key player is a chemical in the brain called CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide). This
chemical is released during migraine attacks and causes inflammation and pain around the
brain.
Hormonal changes can make this process easier to trigger.
What research shows:
● Estrogen affects how pain signals move in the brain.
● When estrogen drops, pain pathways become more active.
● This makes the brain more likely to react strongly to things like stress, lack of sleep,
hunger, or strong smells.
In simple terms, hormonal changes can lower the brain’s pain threshold, meaning things that
wouldn’t normally cause a migraine can suddenly trigger one.
This helps explain why a woman might tolerate stress well at one time of the month, but get a
migraine from the same stress at another time.
Everyday Triggers That Affect Women More
Hormones may set the stage, but everyday life often pulls the trigger. Many things women deal
with daily can make migraines more frequent or worse.
Some common triggers include:
1. Stress: Work pressure, family responsibilities, and emotional stress can easily trigger
migraines.

2. Poor or irregular sleep: Sleeping too little or too much can affect the brain.

3. Skipping meals: Long hours without food can drop blood sugar and trigger attacks.

4. Strong smells: Perfumes, fuel, cleaning chemicals, or cooking fumes.

5. Weather changes: Heat, humidity, or sudden rain, something many women are very
familiar with.
Women often juggle multiple roles at once, and this constant demand on the body and mind can
increase migraine frequency, especially when combined with hormonal changes.
Why Tracking Your Cycle and Migraines Matters
Many women treat migraines as something that just “comes and goes,” but paying attention to
when they happen can be very helpful.
Because hormones play such a big role, migraines often follow a pattern linked to the menstrual
cycle or major life stages.
Keeping track helps you:
● Notice if migraines come before or during your period
● See if they worsen during stressful weeks
● Identify triggers like skipped meals, poor sleep, or heat
● Know when to prepare ahead of time
It can be as simple as noting the date, how bad the pain was, and what was happening around
that time.
When women bring this information to a doctor, it becomes easier to:
● Confirm if the migraine is hormone-related
● Choose better treatment options
● Avoid unnecessary medications that may not help
When you know your own pattern, it puts you back in control.
How Women Can Reduce Migraine Attacks
While you can’t always control hormones, there are steps that can help reduce how often
migraines happen and how severe they get.
Tips that can help:
1. Track your cycle and migraines: Knowing patterns helps you prepare and prevent
attacks.

2. Manage stress: Simple things like short breaks, deep breathing, or light exercise can
make a difference.

3. Prioritize sleep: Aim for regular sleep times and enough rest each night.

4. Eat regularly: Don’t skip meals, and stay hydrated.

5. Avoid known triggers: These could include strong smells, bright lights, or certain foods
that tend to trigger your migraines.

6. Talk to a doctor: Sometimes preventive medications or hormone-based treatments are
needed, especially if migraines follow your menstrual cycle.
Conclusion
Migraines can be tough, especially when they come at certain times in life.
Paying attention to your body, hormones, and daily habits can make managing them a bit easier.
I’d love to hear from you: have you noticed patterns in your migraines, or found ways to reduce
attacks?
Share your thoughts or experiences in the comments. Your story could help another woman
going through the same thing.



Researched by Victoria Odueso

title: Why You Might Feel Bloated
content:
Title: Why You Might Feel Bloated

Keywords: bloating, aerophagia, premenstrual bloating, constipation, food intolerance, fermented foods, Nigerian diet, digestion

Short Description: Learn about the leading causes of bloating and easy ways to ease it with simple diet and lifestyle changes.

Why You Might Feel Bloated

"Discover common causes of bloating, from diet to digestion issues, and learn simple tips to ease discomfort and improve gut health naturally."

Bloating is a common and uncomfortable feeling of fullness or tightness in the belly. This sensation might happen so often for many women that it feels normal.

It might come with symptoms like excessive gas, burping, or abdominal pain.

However, while occasional bloating isn't usually a concern, frequent bloating may signal a deeper issue.

Several factors could be behind that bloated belly, from what you eat and how you live, to your hormones and gut health.

Let's break down the possible causes and what you can do to feel better.

1). Digestive Delays

Food moving slowly through your digestive tract can cause a buildup of gas and pressure. This slow movement is often the result of constipation, which can cause your belly to feel stiff and swollen.

Some foods, such as beans, lentils, broccoli, onions, and cabbage, contain fermentable carbohydrates known as FODMAPs, which tend to produce gas during digestion. If you're sensitive to FODMAPs, your gut may struggle to break them down, leading to bloating, gas, and discomfort.

In other cases, you might be experiencing gastroparesis, a condition where your stomach empties more slowly than normal. This is often seen in people with diabetes or those recovering from surgery.

2). Swallowing Excess Air

You may not realize it, but simple actions like chewing gum, drinking fizzy drinks, or eating too quickly can cause you to swallow excess air—a condition known as aerophagia. This air can become trapped in your digestive tract, leading to bloating.

Habits like sipping from straws, smoking, or talking while eating increase the amount of air that enters your system. Once trapped, this air can create pressure in the abdomen, making it feel like you're carrying a balloon inside your stomach.

3). Food Intolerances

If you regularly feel bloated after meals, your body might be reacting to certain foods it can't digest properly. Lactose intolerance occurs when your body lacks the enzyme needed to break down lactose, the sugar in milk. When undigested lactose reaches your colon, it is fermented by bacteria, releasing gas.

Gluten sensitivity or celiac disease can also cause bloating. For those with celiac disease, gluten triggers an immune response that damages the small intestine, interfering with nutrient absorption and causing bloating, diarrhea, and fatigue.

If you notice bloating after eating dairy, bread, or processed foods, you might want to try cutting out certain foods with a doctor's help to see if it helps.

4). Premenstrual Bloating

Hormonal fluctuations during your menstrual cycle can lead to water retention and slowed digestion, which can result in bloating.

In the days leading up to your period, levels of estrogen and progesterone change, affecting how your body manages fluid and digestion.

These hormonal shifts can also cause increased gas and constipation. While uncomfortable, this type of bloating is temporary and typically subsides once your period begins.

Reducing intake of salty foods and caffeine during your cycle and staying hydrated can help alleviate premenstrual bloating.

5). Gut Imbalance

A healthy digestive system is home to trillions of bacteria, known as the gut microbiome, which help break down food and support immune function. But when this balance is disrupted by stress, poor diet, or antibiotics, it can lead to gut dysbiosis and bloating.

Too many gas-producing bacteria in your small intestine can lead to small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). This condition often causes bloating soon after eating, abdominal discomfort, and changes in bowel habits.

Fermented foods like nunu (fermented milk), ogi (fermented maize pudding), ugba (fermented oil bean seed), and iru (fermented locust beans) can help restore gut balance and reduce bloating over time, thanks to their natural probiotic content.

6). Stress and Anxiety

Emotional stress doesn't just affect your mind; it also impacts your gut. The gut-brain connection means your digestive system responds to your emotional state. When you're stressed, digestion slows, which can lead to bloating, cramping, and constipation.

Stress can also increase sensitivity to gas and discomfort, making minor bloating feel much worse than it is. Practices like deep breathing, journaling, and getting enough sleep can support better gut health and reduce symptoms over time.

7). Overeating or Eating Too Fast

Eating large meals or eating too fast can overwhelm your digestive system. When you eat quickly, your brain doesn't have enough time to register fullness, causing you to consume more than your body needs. This leads to excessive food and gas in the gut, which causes bloating.

Chewing food thoroughly and practicing mindful eating give your digestive system time to keep up with what you're eating, reducing the risk of post-meal bloating.

8). Water Retention and Sodium

When your body holds on to excess fluid, it can cause bloating and puffiness, especially around your belly. This is often linked to excessive salt intake, which disrupts your body's fluid balance.

Processed snacks, instant noodles, and canned soups often contain high levels of sodium.

If your diet is heavy on salty or packaged foods, consider increasing your potassium intake with foods like bananas, sweet potatoes, or avocados to help your body balance fluids.

9). Medical Conditions

Sometimes, bloating is a sign of an underlying health condition that needs medical attention. These can include:

  • Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), which causes bloating, cramps, diarrhea, or constipation.
  • Endometriosis, a condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus and causes pelvic pain, bloating, and heavy periods.
  • Ovarian cysts or fibroids can create a feeling of pressure or fullness in the lower abdomen.
  • Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), like Crohn's or ulcerative colitis, which inflames the digestive tract and leads to bloating, weight loss, and fatigue.

Persistent or painful bloating should never be ignored, especially when accompanied by weight changes, severe cramps, or blood in your stool. A doctor can help identify the root cause and offer treatment options.

10). Dehydration and Low Fiber

Not drinking enough water can cause your body to retain water, leading to bloating. When you're dehydrated, your system slows down digestion, and waste moves sluggishly through your intestines.

On the flip side, a low-fiber diet can lead to constipation and a backed-up gut. Fiber adds bulk to your stool and helps it pass more easily, but adding too much too quickly can also cause gas.

A gradual increase, along with plenty of water, helps reduce bloating and keeps digestion smooth.

When to See a Doctor

While bloating is often benign, certain situations require medical attention. You should consult a doctor if:

  • Bloating is persistent or severe and interferes with daily life.
  • Other symptoms are present, such as bloody stools, changes in bowel habits, unexplained weight loss, constipation, diarrhea, or persistent nausea. These could indicate severe conditions like ovarian cancer, colon cancer, or inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Immediate care is needed for prolonged abdominal pain or chest pain, which could signal a medical emergency.

Keeping a symptom diary, noting when bloating occurs and any associated symptoms, can help your doctor identify the cause and recommend appropriate tests, such as blood tests, imaging, or a hydrogen breath test, for conditions like fructose malabsorption.


What You Can Do to Feel Better

If bloating is becoming a regular visitor, these habits can help bring relief:

  • Eat slowly and mindfully, giving your body time to digest and reducing the air you swallow.
  • Watch for personal trigger foods like dairy, bread, beans, or highly processed snacks, especially if you're sensitive to lactose, gluten, or FODMAPs.
  • Stay hydrated, as water keeps things moving and helps prevent constipation.
  • Move your body daily—even a short walk after meals can ease digestion.
  • Add fermented foods to your meals. Nigerian options like nunu, ogi, ugba, and iru naturally support gut health with beneficial bacteria (learn more here).

If you're unsure what's causing your bloating, or if it becomes a regular issue, it's okay to ask for help.

There's no one-size-fits-all solution, but with some observation and minor adjustments, you can start feeling better from the inside out.

Final Thoughts

Your gut is more connected to your well-being than you might think.

By treating it with care, you're not just easing discomfort but promoting your body's overall health, comfort, and long-term wellness.

title: Why You Shouldn’t Ignore Sores or Itching Around Your Anus
content:
Title:
Why You Shouldn't Ignore Sores or Itching Around Your Anus

Keywords:
anal itching, anal sores, female STIs, HPV symptoms, genital warts, herpes, anal discomfort, women's sexual health, STI warning signs

Short Description:
Itching or sores around your anus may seem minor, but they can be early signs of STIs, HPV, or other health issues. Here's what you need to know, when to see a doctor, and why early care matters.

Why You Shouldn't Ignore Sores or Itching Around Your Anus

Itching or sores around the anus might seem like a minor issue, maybe you think it's from sweat, shaving, or tight underwear. But sometimes, it's not that simple. It could be your body's way of signalling that something isn't right.

Many women ignore symptoms like anal itching, soreness, or small bumps, often due to discomfort or embarrassment.

But these signs shouldn't be dismissed. They can point to a sexually transmitted infection (STI), a viral outbreak like herpes, or even something more serious, such as HPV-related anal cancer.

If you're sexually active, this is something you need to pay attention to.

What Could Be Causing It?

Several conditions can cause itching, sores, or discomfort around the anus, ranging from mild to more serious. Common causes include:

1. Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
Infections like herpes, syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and HPV can all cause itching, bumps, or ulcers around the anal area.

Many people don't show symptoms immediately, but the virus or bacteria can still spread and cause damage.

2. Anal Fissures or Haemorrhoids
These can develop from constipation, straining, or irritation and may be mistaken for STI symptoms.

3. Genital or Anal Warts (HPV)
These are soft, skin-coloured growths that can appear around the anus or genitals. They may itch, bleed, or go unnoticed entirely.

4. Fungal or Bacterial Infections
Moisture, poor hygiene, or prolonged discharge can lead to fungal growth, which may cause itching and irritation.

5. Parasitic Infections (e.g., Pinworms)
While more common in children, adults can still get pinworms, which often cause nighttime anal itching.

Why You Shouldn't Wait

When you ignore these signs, things can deteriorate rapidly.

  • STIs can quietly spread, damaging your reproductive organs or making you more vulnerable to other infections.
  • Untreated anal warts from HPV can develop into precancerous or cancerous growths.
  • Sores or bleeding that don't heal may indicate that something more serious is occurring.

Many women only seek help when the pain becomes unbearable or when the infection has already spread. Don't let it get to that point.

When to See a Doctor

Please don't wait weeks or months hoping it clears up on its own. See a doctor if you notice:

  • Itching or burning that won't stop
  • Sores, ulcers, or small growths around the anus or genitals
  • Bleeding when you're not on your period
  • Pain during sex or when using the toilet
  • Any discharge or smell that feels unusual

Even if it feels small, it's better to confirm than to assume.

What to Expect at the Clinic

Your doctor may:

  • Take a look at the area
  • Use a swab or sample to test for infections
  • Do an anoscopy to look inside the anus if needed
  • Suggest a biopsy if something doesn't look normal

The process is usually quick, and in most cases, you get answers within a few days.

Treatment Options

Once the cause is confirmed, treatment can begin immediately. This might include:

  • Antibiotics or antivirals for bacterial or viral infections
  • Topical creams for itching, rashes, or fungal infections
  • Cryotherapy or minor procedures to remove warts
  • Guidance on hygiene, protection, and follow-up care

The earlier you treat it, the faster you heal and the lower your risk of complications.

How to Prevent It

  • Use condoms, including during anal sex
  • Avoid sharing sex toys without proper cleaning
  • Get tested regularly if you're sexually active
  • Clean the area gently and avoid perfumed soaps or wipes.
  • Stay dry, especially during hot weather or long periods of discharge

Final Word

If something feels off, don't dismiss it. That little itch, bump, or sore might be more than just a skin reaction.

Get it checked. Treat it early. Protect yourself and your partner.

And if you've noticed anything like this before or have questions, but are unsure who to ask, feel free to drop them here with no judgment. Let's talk about it.

Researched by Victoria Odueso

title: How can women break free from people-pleasing habits
content:
Title:

How Can Women Break Free from People-Pleasing Habits

Keywords:
people-pleasing, Nigerian women, emotional wellbeing, boundaries, self-esteem, assertiveness, mental health, self-care, confidence, saying no

Short Description:

This article takes a look at why women fall into people-pleasing habits, how it affects their emotional wellbeing, and simple, realistic steps to break free, from learning to say no without guilt, to choosing peace over approval.

How can women break free from people-pleasing habits?

From church committees to family gatherings, many women find themselves saying, “It’s fine,” even when it’s clearly not.

You agree to help your colleague after work, attend a friend’s event even when you’re drained, or take on family responsibilities you can’t handle, all because you don’t want to offend anyone.

This constant need to keep everyone happy is what psychologists call people-pleasing, putting others’ comfort above your own peace.

It’s something many of us learned growing up, where being a “good girl” meant being quiet, respectful, and available to everyone at all times.

But at what point does being nice start becoming a burden on your mental health and happiness?

Learning to stop people-pleasing isn’t rebellion; it’s self-respect.

Why We Fall Into People-Pleasing (and Don’t Even Realise It)

  • Upbringing: Many of us grew up being told to “don’t argue,” or “just do it so they won’t say you’re rude.” Over time, you may start to believe that saying no or speaking up makes you a bad person.
  • Fear of being misunderstood: You don’t want people to think you’re proud, difficult, or disrespectful, especially in settings like family, work, or church. So, you keep saying yes even.
  • Desire for love and approval: Deep down, you want people to like you. You want peace in your relationships, so you do whatever it takes to avoid conflict, even if it means sacrificing your own comfort.
  • Guilt: When you finally try to say no or put yourself first, you feel bad, like you’ve disappointed someone. That guilt pushes you right back into saying yes again.
  • Cultural and religious expectations: Society praises women who sacrifice, serve, and “endure.” Saying no can be mistaken for pride or rebellion.

At the heart of it, people-pleasing is often rooted in fear, fear of being misunderstood, unloved, or abandoned.

But the truth is, you don’t have to earn respect by over-giving or over-explaining.

Research on approval addiction supports this: people who excessively seek approval tend to suffer from low self-esteem and define their worth based on how others view them.

Signs You’re a People-Pleaser

Sometimes, we don’t even realise we’re people-pleasing, it just feels like being “nice” or “helpful.”

But there’s a big difference between being kind and losing yourself trying to keep everyone happy.

Here are a few signs to watch out for:

  • You say “yes” even when you’re tired or already overwhelmed.
  • You apologise for things that aren’t your fault, just to avoid conflict.
  • You feel anxious or guilty when someone is upset with you.
  • You find it hard to express your real opinion if it might cause disagreement.
  • You often do favours for people who wouldn’t do the same for you.
  • You feel drained or resentful after constantly giving and never receiving.

If you see yourself in some of these, don’t beat yourself up. Many of us were raised this way, to keep the peace at all costs. The good news? You can unlearn it.

Awareness is the first step toward change.

The Price You Pay for Always Saying “Yes”

  • Constant tiredness: You’re always running around trying to meet everyone’s expectations, leaving little time to rest or focus on yourself.
  • Feeling invisible: People start taking your kindness for granted because you never complain or set limits.
  • Emotional buildup: You smile on the outside but quietly feel angry or resentful because no one seems to care how you feel.
  • Loss of confidence: You begin to doubt your own needs and choices since you’re used to putting others first.

It’s like pouring from an empty cup; no matter how much you give, it never feels enough. And in the end, you lose touch with who you truly are.

Steps to Start Breaking Free

Breaking free from people-pleasing doesn’t happen overnight, but small, consistent changes can make a big difference.

The goal isn’t to stop being kind, but to start being kind to yourself, too.

Here’s how to start:

1. Notice your patterns

Pay attention to moments when you say yes out of guilt or fear.

Ask yourself: “Do I really want to do this, or am I just afraid of disappointing someone?”

Writing down these moments helps you see how often it happens.

2. Practice Saying “No” Without Feeling Guilty

You don’t owe everyone an explanation. Try calm, polite responses like:

  • “I’d love to, but I can’t right now.”
  • “Let me get back to you.”
  • “I don’t have the capacity for that at the moment.”

Start small, maybe say no to a request that drains you, and it’ll get easier with time.

3. Set Boundaries, Even With Loved Ones

Boundaries are not pride or stubbornness; they’re self-respect. It’s okay to rest, to say you’re busy, or to ask for space when you need it.

If someone truly loves and respects you, they’ll understand

4. Learn to Approve Yourself

Don’t wait for others to clap for you before you feel worthy.

Speak kindly to yourself, celebrate your small wins, and stop measuring your worth by people’s opinions.

Self-acceptance takes practice, but it’s the surest way to freedom.

5. Stop Feeling Guilty for Resting

Rest isn’t laziness, it’s necessary. You don’t have to earn rest by overworking or pleasing others first.

6. Surround Yourself With Supportive People

Spend more time with people who respect your “no.” Watch how they confidently and without guilt handle boundaries.

The more you see it modeled, the easier it becomes to do the same.

Final Thoughts

At the end of the day, you owe yourself the same care and respect you freely give to others. You don’t have to shrink yourself to be accepted or exhaust yourself to be valued.

Peace feels unfamiliar at first, especially if you’ve lived your whole life pleasing others, but with time, it becomes a sense of freedom.

What about you?

Have you ever struggled with people-pleasing or found a way to overcome it? I’d love to hear your thoughts or personal experiences.

Researched by Victoria Odueso

title: How to Calm Yourself During a Panic Attack
content:
Title: How to Calm Yourself During a Panic Attack

Keywords: panic attack, anxiety, breathing techniques, grounding methods, relaxation, self-talk, cold water, panic disorder support

Short Description:
Panic attacks can feel overwhelming, but they are manageable. This article shares simple, evidence-based techniques you can use to calm yourself when panic strikes and regain control in the moment.

How to Calm Yourself During a Panic Attack

If you’ve ever had a panic attack, you know how terrifying it feels. Your chest tightens, your heart races, and for a moment it seems like you’re completely losing control.

The good news is: as scary as they feel, panic attacks are not dangerous. They happen when your body’s “fight-or-flight” response becomes overactive, often triggered by stress or sometimes without a clear cause.

It usually passes within minutes, and there are simple things you can do to help yourself through it.

Let’s take a look at them.

1. Recognize That It’s a Panic Attack

One of the quickest ways to lower the intensity of a panic attack is to recognize it for what it is.

Panic attacks feel frightening, but they are not life-threatening. Understanding this reduces the “fear of fear” that often fuels the cycle.

Common symptoms include:

  • Racing heartbeat
  • Shortness of breath
  • Dizziness or trembling
  • Sweating or chills
  • A feeling of losing control

People who can correctly identify their symptoms as a panic attack experience less escalation of fear.

This is because the brain stops interpreting the sensations as dangerous, such as a heart attack or fainting spell.

2. Focus on Your Breathing

When panic sets in, many people begin breathing too fast and shallowly.

This makes the chest feel tighter, the head lightheaded, and the fear even worse. Slowing your breathing helps your body calm down and steadies your mind.

  • Try this technique: Inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 7 seconds, then exhale slowly for 8 seconds (4-7-8 Method).
  • Alternate: Place a hand on your belly and breathe deeply, letting it rise and fall. This encourages calmer, diaphragmatic breathing.

Research confirms that slow, controlled breathing significantly reduces anxiety symptoms by activating the body’s relaxation response (parasympathetic system) and lowering physiological arousal.

3. Ground Yourself in the Present (5-4-3-2-1 Method)

When panic hits, your mind often races into “what ifs.” Grounding helps pull you back to the Present, reminding your brain that you are safe.

The 5-4-3-2-1 Method:

  • 5 things you can see
  • 4 things you can touch
  • 3 things you can hear
  • 2 things you can smell
  • 1 thing you can taste

Why it works: This exercise engages your senses, shifts focus from fear to reality, and reduces the intensity of anxious thoughts.

Grounding techniques help regulate overwhelming emotions, reduce dissociation, and bring calm during anxiety or panic.

4. Relax Your Body

Panic attacks often make your muscles tighten without you even noticing. Releasing that tension sends a signal of safety back to your brain.

  • Drop your shoulders away from your ears.
  • Unclench your fists and jaw.
  • If possible, try progressive muscle relaxation: tense one muscle group (like your hands) for a few seconds, then release. Move through your body from head to toe.

Progressive muscle relaxation reduces physical tension and lowers anxiety symptoms, making it easier to regain control during a panic episode.

5. Use Reassuring Self-talk

What you say to yourself during a panic attack matters. Negative thoughts like “I’m losing control” can fuel the panic, while calm reminders can help ease it.

Try phrases such as:

  • “This will pass.”
  • “I am safe.”
  • “My body is just reacting, but I am okay.”

Cognitive-behavioral research suggests that replacing catastrophic thoughts with realistic ones can reduce the intensity of panic symptoms and help interrupt the fear cycle.

6. Splash Cold Water or Hold an Ice Cube

Cold sensations can interrupt a panic attack by quickly shifting your body’s focus.

  • Splash cool water on your face.
  • Hold an ice cube in your hand and notice the sharp, cold feeling.
  • Place a cold cloth on the back of your neck.

This works because a sudden cold can activate the body’s “diving reflex,” which naturally slows the heart rate and calms the nervous system.

What to do If Panic Attacks Happen Often

If panic attacks keep repeating, it may help to look at patterns in your lifestyle and seek extra support.

i. Keep a diary: Track when attacks happen, what you were doing, and how you felt. This can reveal triggers.

ii. Lifestyle support:

  • Regular exercise
  • Consistent sleep
  • Cutting back on caffeine or alcohol

iii. Professional help

If attacks are frequent or interfering with daily life, talking to a mental health professional can make a big difference. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and, in some cases, medication are proven treatments for panic disorder.

Summary

Remember, panic attacks do not define who you are. With time and practice, you can build confidence in handling them and continue living fully.

If you’ve had your own experience when you had a panic attack at one point in time, please share it below. Someone else might draw strength from your story.

Researched by Victoria Odueso

title: How to Deal with Anxiety in High-Pressure Environments
content:
Title: How to Deal with Anxiety in High-Pressure Environments.

Keywords: Anxiety in high-pressure environments, anxiety, stress relief, grounding techniques, coping with pressure, anxiety symptoms, coping with stress.

Short Description: Feeling anxious in high-pressure situations is normal. This guide offers simple techniques and habits to help you stay calm and in control.

How to Deal with Anxiety in High-Pressure Environments

"Get easy tips to stay calm and manage anxiety in stressful or high-pressure situations, so you can feel more in control and do your best."

Anxiety is your body's built-in alarm system. In high-pressure environments, like exams, job interviews, public speaking, or tight work deadlines, it often kicks in to help you focus.

But too much of it? That can leave you feeling overwhelmed, scattered, and stuck.

The truth is, some level of anxiety is natural. But when it starts interfering with your ability to function or perform at your best, it's time to take back control.

Here's a guide to help you understand what's happening in your body and mind, and most importantly, how to manage anxiety effectively in high-pressure environments.

Let's get started!

What Does High-Pressure Anxiety Look Like?

Before you can manage anxiety, you need to identify how it shows up. The signs can vary from one person to another, but common symptoms include:

  • Physical symptoms: racing heart, rapid breathing, tight chest, dizziness, headaches, trembling, nausea, or excessive sweating.
  • Emotional symptoms: irritability, panic, fear, nervousness, or a sense of impending doom.
  • Cognitive symptoms: You might have trouble focusing, forget things easily, think too fast, or expect the worst, like telling yourself, "I'm going to fail" or "This will go terribly."
  • Behavioral symptoms: avoiding tasks, procrastination, over-checking, people-pleasing, or emotional outbursts

Many of these reactions stem from your body's fight-or-flight response. This is a natural way your body tries to keep you safe from danger.

But today, things like exams or work stress can make this system work too hard, even when there's no real danger.

Common Triggers of Performance Anxiety

Knowing your triggers can help you plan for them. Here are common causes of anxiety in high-pressure settings:

  • Fear of failure or rejection
  • Perfectionism and unrealistic standards
  • Comparison with others
  • High expectations from parents, teachers, or employers
  • Lack of preparation
  • Public scrutiny or being judged
  • Previous traumatic experiences
  • Sleep deprivation or poor nutrition

Understanding your triggers doesn't make them disappear, but it gives you the power to prepare and respond mindfully instead of reactively.

What to Do When You Feel Overwhelmed

When anxiety builds up during a stressful moment, these techniques can bring quick relief:

1). Practice deep breathing

Slow, deep breaths signal your brain to calm down. Try inhaling slowly through your nose for 4 seconds, holding for 4 seconds, then exhaling through your mouth for 4 seconds.

This technique, similar to the 4-7-8 breathing method, reduces heart rate and helps you regain focus.

You can also try box breathing (4-4-4-4 method). It is a technique used by athletes and Navy SEALs that helps regulate your breathing and calm your nervous system.

How to do it:

  • Inhale for 4 seconds
  • Hold for 4 seconds
  • Exhale for 4 seconds
  • Hold for another 4 seconds.
  • Repeat 4–6 times.

2). Ground yourself using your senses.

Anxiety often fuels worries about the future or regrets about the past. The 5-4-3-2-1 grounding exercise uses your senses to pull you back to the moment.

Look around and name five things you see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. This exercise interrupts racing thoughts and centers your mind.

Studies show this method slows down racing thoughts and reduces panic symptoms.

3). Relax your muscles

Anxiety tightens muscles, often without you noticing. Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) involves tensing and releasing different muscle groups, starting with your feet and moving upward.

This practice helps ease physical tension and mental stress, especially before presentations, exams, or high-stakes conversations.

Ways to Change Your Thinking to Feel Less Anxious Over Time

1). Reframe Your Thoughts with CBT Techniques

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is one of the most effective ways to treat and manage anxiety. It teaches you how to challenge distorted thoughts like:

  • "If I mess this up, I'm a failure."
  • "Everyone will think I'm incompetent."
  • "This pressure is too much for me."

CBT helps you reframe them into realistic beliefs:

  • "Mistakes don't define me."
  • "I can prepare and give my best."
  • "Pressure means this matters, not that I can't handle it."

2). Self-Compassion Over Perfectionism

Practicing self-compassion is about treating yourself like you'd treat a friend. It reduces shame and builds resilience.
Instead of beating yourself up after a rough performance, try saying: "That was tough, but I showed up. I'm proud of that."

Long-Term Habits to Reduce Anxiety

Managing anxiety goes beyond handling immediate symptoms. Building daily habits that support mental health strengthens your ability to handle pressure:


1). Maintain a Balanced Diet

Nutrients affect brain chemistry and mood. Eating foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids, B vitamins, and antioxidants supports mental health.

That's because your gut and brain are closely connected, and a healthy gut can help reduce anxiety.

Fermented foods and probiotics, like yogurt or Nigerian staples like fermented ogi or kunu, can positively influence gut-brain communication and reduce anxiety symptoms.

Try to cut back on processed sugar, caffeine, and alcohol, as they can make anxiety worse.

2). Prioritize good sleep

Sleep deprivation worsens anxiety by impairing your brain's ability to regulate emotions.

Following good sleep hygiene, such as going to bed at the same time every night and avoiding screens before sleep, improves rest and emotional resilience.

3). Stay active

Exercise is a natural anxiety reliever. Aerobic activities like walking, dancing, or skipping release mood-enhancing chemicals called endorphins, which improve mood and reduce stress.

4). Limit stimulants

Caffeine and energy drinks can increase heart rate and nervousness, which may worsen anxiety. Consider replacing them with herbal teas like chamomile or zobo (hibiscus tea), which have calming properties.

5). Practice Time Management

Break big tasks into smaller steps to make them easier to handle. Use a digital planner or a paper to-do list to stay organized. Don't forget to include break times.

Managing your time well helps you avoid last-minute stress and do a better job.

6). Create a Supportive Environment

High-pressure environments don't always allow complete control, but you can build a support system that helps you thrive within them.

  • Talk to someone: Venting to a trusted friend, sibling, mentor, or colleague can lighten emotional pressure.
  • Join a support group: Find people going through similar challenges. Shared experiences reduce isolation.
  • Get accommodations: Students or employees with chronic anxiety can request reasonable accommodations, such as extended deadlines or quiet workspaces.

If anxiety affects your daily functioning or becomes chronic, consider seeing a licensed therapist or mental health provider.

7). Try Journaling to Unload Mental Clutter

Journaling helps you process emotions, untangle thoughts, and track progress.

Try one of these journaling prompts when pressure builds up:

  • What's really bothering me right now?
  • What would I say to a friend in this situation?
  • What can I control, and what can I release?
  • What evidence do I have that things could go well?

Even 5 minutes a day can help improve clarity and lower stress levels.

8). Use Affirmations and Visualization

Positive affirmations rewire your internal dialogue. Choose statements that feel true and empowering.

Examples:

  • "I can do hard things."
  • "Pressure means growth, not defeat."
  • "I don't need to be perfect, I just need to show up."

Use affirmations along with visualization, picture yourself doing well in a meeting, exam, or presentation. This helps build confidence and reduces anxiety.

9). Make time for relaxation

Engage in activities that soothe your mind, such as listening to music, practicing meditation, praying, or engaging in hobbies you enjoy.

These moments of calm aren't indulgent; they're essential to maintaining balance.

Final Notes

You're not weak because you feel anxious in high-pressure situations. You're human.

And with the right tools, self-awareness, and support systems, you can stay grounded, even when life gets intense.

Anxiety may not disappear overnight, but it doesn't have to take over your life.

Researched by Victoria Odueso

title: WE ARE JUST TIRED
content:
Title:
We Are Just Tired
Keywords:
tiredness, exhaustion, mental health, coping strategies, Nigeria, workplace stress, daily
pressures, burnout, resilience, fatigue, societal expectations, stress management, limited
support, personal wellbeing
Short Description:
This article explores why people feel constantly exhausted, the daily pressures that contribute to
burnout, the challenges in accessing mental health support, and the ways people cope when
formal help is scarce. It highlights the personal and systemic impact of chronic tiredness and
suggests steps for managing it.











WE ARE JUST TIRED
Lately, it feels like everyone is tired.
Not the kind of tired that sleep fixes. The kind that stays with you through the day. The kind you
carry while replying to messages, sitting in traffic, meeting deadlines, and pretending you’re fine.
You hear it in sighs before voice notes. You see it in slow replies and missed calls. You feel it
when simple things take too much effort.
For many, life has become a constant management task. Managing money. Managing work.
Managing expectations. Even rest feels rushed.
And still, the message is the same: keep going. Be strong. Handle it.
So people do. They endure. They adjust. They survive. But over time, that survival turns into
exhaustion.
This piece looks at where that tiredness comes from, why help is hard to find, how people are
coping, and what happens when coping is all there is.
Because when everyone feels this way, it stops being personal.
Where the Exhaustion Is Coming From
This tiredness doesn’t come from one thing. It builds from pressures happening at the same
time. Most days start before the body is ready and end long after the mind has shut down.
Some of the pressures that pile up include:
1. Money stress: Salaries that barely cover rent, transport, school fees, and groceries.
Side hustles are no longer optional; they are necessary.
2. Work pressure: Long hours, constant availability, impossible targets. Expectations
rarely pause for your energy levels.
3. Commute stress: Hours lost in traffic. Leaving home early. Getting back late. Starting
and ending the day already drained.
4. Social comparison: Seeing others relocate, get new jobs, or “figure life out” online while
you feel stuck.
On top of that, society pushes the same message:
● Being tired is a weakness
● Rest feels like laziness
● Saying “I’m struggling” feels risky
● Smiling and managing becomes the default

Women often feel this more sharply: work responsibilities rarely reduce home expectations.
Emotional support is expected. Strength is assumed.
How the Body Reacts
Over time, this pressure affects the body and mind in several ways. Like you:
● Waking up tired even after sleep
● Losing focus or motivation
● Short patience and irritability
● Skipping meals or living on caffeine
● Putting personal care and rest aside
● Feeling like you’re always behind.
Why Help Is Hard to Find
When this tiredness turns into something heavier, affecting your sleep, mood, or focus, you
might start to think: Maybe I should get help.
Then reality hits. In Nigeria, help is often hard to reach. Even when people know they need
support, the options are limited, expensive, and far away.
Awareness Exists, But Access Lags
People are talking about mental health more than before. There are:
● Online communities and WhatsApp groups
● Social media hashtags and campaigns
● Occasional wellbeing workshops in schools or offices
People can name stress, burnout, and fatigue. They know it affects the body and mind.
But knowing is not the same as getting help. Awareness has moved faster than access.
Mental Health Services Are Limited
Even in big cities in Lagos:
● Psychologists and psychiatrists are few; one counsellor may serve hundreds of people
● Clinics are often in expensive areas with hours that clash with work
● Appointments can take weeks, sometimes months
● Fees are high and often unaffordable
And outside major cities, these options are almost non-existent.

Workplaces Aren’t Much Better
Offices often fail to support employees properly:
● Long hours, back-to-back meetings, and high performance expectations
● HR may mention wellness programs or counselling on paper, but rarely make them
accessible
● Sessions can be during work hours, limited in number, or stigmatized, making staff
reluctant to attend
For many, exhaustion meets bureaucracy at work. People are expected to keep performing, no
matter how drained they feel.
How We’re Managing and Sometimes Struggling
When formal support is out of reach, people find ways to get by. Some of it works. Some of it
doesn’t.
Small Ways We Cope
● Short breaks: Stepping away from a screen or a task for a few minutes to breathe or
stretch
● Laughter: Joking with colleagues, friends, or family to release tension
● Confiding in others: Sharing feelings with someone trusted
● Music, podcasts, or TV: Temporary escape from stress
● Using meditation or wellness apps
● Self-medicating without guidance
These actions don’t fix the root problem, but they help people keep going for the day.
Riskier Habits
● Skipping meals or relying too much on caffeine to stay awake
● Pushing through illness or pain to meet work deadlines
● Withdrawing from friends or family when drained
● Over-relying on self-help routines without professional guidance
These habits are understandable; they make sense in the moment, but if repeated over weeks
or months, they can worsen exhaustion, affect health, and strain relationships.
Workplace Strain
At work, coping often means hiding struggles:
● Pushing through fatigue while trying to meet expectations

● Avoiding counselling or HR programs due to stigma or inconvenient timing
● Appearing “fine” even when mentally or physically drained
Managers may praise endurance, thereby normalizing exhaustion. For many, survival in the
office becomes a skill rather than a choice.
When Coping Becomes a Risk
Managing daily fatigue only works up to a point. Over time, the shortcuts, small breaks, and
improvisations stop being enough.
Health and Body
● Chronic exhaustion can lead to headaches, back pain, digestive issues, and weakened
immunity.
● Mental strain can become anxiety, depression, or burnout.
● Skipping meals, overworking, and constant stress affect sleep, focus, and overall energy.
Work and Productivity
● Pushing through fatigue reduces efficiency and creativity.
● Errors increase, deadlines are harder to meet, and opportunities are missed.
● Offices may notice “resilient employees,” but resilience here is forced, not healthy.
Family and Relationships
● Tiredness spreads. Irritability or withdrawal affects partners, children, and extended
family.
● Caregiving responsibilities may clash with personal limits, causing friction and frustration
at home.
Communities and Society
● Those outside major cities face almost no support, widening inequality.
● Exhaustion becomes shared: workplaces, families, and communities all feel the strain.
What appears to be endurance or resilience is often forced adaptation. People manage
because they must, not because it’s optional. Survival becomes a constant, and the cost is
visible in health, relationships, and daily life.

What We Can Do About It
At Home
● Set boundaries: Give yourself time to rest without guilt.
● Share responsibilities: Split chores, caregiving, and daily tasks with family when
possible.
● Notice your limits: It’s okay to say no or postpone a task.
At Work
● Use available support: Employee Assistance Programs or counselling services, even if
limited, are worth trying.
● Talk to HR: Push for flexible hours, wellbeing initiatives, or realistic workloads.
● Small pauses matter: Step away for a few minutes, stretch, or take a walk to reset your
mind.
Personal Habits
● Rest when you can: Even short naps or a calm evening routine help.
● Healthy basics: Food, water, sleep, and movement are not luxuries; they’re survival
tools.
● Lean on trusted people: Friends, family, or community networks can help you cope
safely.
● Spiritual routines: Prayer, reflection, or meditation can provide real comfort and
renewal, helping you regain energy and perspective during exhaustion.
Looking Ahead
Exhaustion is not just personal. It reflects how life, work, and systems are structured.
Awareness is growing, and conversations about stress, mental health, and wellbeing are
happening, but action is needed.
Even small steps, repeated consistently, can change the experience of everyday life. Pausing,
asking for help, and sharing the load aren’t weaknesses; they’re strengths. And strength
becomes stronger when it’s shared.
I want to hear from you: What small changes have helped you manage your tiredness? Or
what do you wish could change in your work, home, or daily life to make things easier?


Written by Victoria Odueso

title: Can I use mild soap on my vagina
content:
Title:
Can I Use Mild Soap on My Vagina?

Keywords:
vagina, vulva, mild soap, vaginal hygiene, intimate care, vaginal pH, discharge, irritation, infection, feminine health

Short Description:
Many women wonder if it’s safe to use soap on the vagina. This article explains the difference between the vagina and vulva, why the vagina cleans itself, the risks of using soap, and safer hygiene tips every woman should know.

Can I use mild soap on my vagina?

Many of us often wonder if it’s safe to use soap on the vagina. It’s a common concern, especially with all the ads for feminine washes and scented soaps.

The first thing to know is that the vagina (the internal part) is different from the vulva (the outer skin and folds).

Using soap inside can upset the vagina’s balance and cause problems, but the outside area can be cleaned gently with water, and in some cases, a mild, unscented soap may be used.

To understand why soap isn’t needed inside, let’s look at how the vagina naturally keeps itself clean.

How the Vagina Cleanses Itself

  • Natural discharge: The vagina produces clear or whitish discharge that helps wash away dead cells and bacteria.
  • Healthy bacteria (lactobacilli): These maintain a slightly acidic pH (3.8–4.5), which helps protect against infections.
  • Self-regulation: This natural system keeps the vagina clean without the need for soap or special products.

Because of this built-in balance, adding soap or chemicals inside can disrupt the process and lead to irritation or infection.

Can Mild Soap Be Used?

a. Inside the vagina: No. Even mild soaps can upset the pH balance, kill healthy bacteria, and cause irritation or infection.

b. On the vulva (outside area): Yes, but only with caution. If you feel uncomfortable using only water, the safest option is:

  • Plain, unscented soap (no perfume, dyes, or antiseptics).
  • Non-antibacterial and non-foaming cleansers.
  • Use small amounts, applied by hand, and rinse thoroughly.

Avoid:

  • Perfumed soaps, body washes, and bubble baths.
  • “Feminine washes” and douching products.
  • Antiseptic solutions (e.g., Dettol, Savlon).

These products often do more harm than good. Water alone is often enough to keep the vulva clean and healthy.

Risks of Using Some Soaps and Harsh Products

  • Irritation and dryness – soaps strip away natural oils, leaving the skin sensitive.
  • Itching or burning – especially with fragranced or antiseptic soaps.
  • Infections – disrupting the natural pH may increase the risk of bacterial vaginosis or yeast infections.
  • Allergic reactions – ingredients like perfumes, dyes, or antiseptics can trigger contact dermatitis.

How to Wash Properly (Step-by-Step)

  • Wash your hands first.
  • Stand or sit in the shower.
  • Use water and your clean hand (avoid using a sponge, loofah, or washcloth).
  • If you choose soap, lather a small amount on your hand.
  • Gently wash the outer folds (labia majora and labia minora), moving front to back.
  • Rinse thoroughly with water.
  • Pat dry with a soft towel, being careful not to rub too hard.

This method reduces the risk of irritation and maintains the natural balance.

Special Situations

  • During pregnancy: Stick to water or very mild soap. Avoid douching completely, as it increases the risk of complications.
  • After your period: Water is usually enough. Avoid using perfumed washes or sprays to mask odour.
  • After sex: Passing urine and washing the vulva gently with water is enough to stay clean and reduce infection risk.
  • If you have sensitive skin/eczema: Doctors often recommend soap substitutes like emollient creams or ointments instead of regular soap.

When to See a Doctor

See a healthcare professional if you notice:

  • Unusual or excessive discharge(thick, yellow, green, or clumpy).
  • Strong or foul odor
  • Persistent itching or burning
  • Pain during sex or urination
  • Unexplained sores, rashes, or bleeding

These may be signs of an infection or another condition that needs medical care.

Conclusion

Health conversations like this remind us that knowledge is power. Many women grow up with little or no guidance on these issues, so it’s easy to pick up habits that may not be safe.

Talking openly and learning the right information helps us care for ourselves with confidence and avoid unnecessary worries.

title: Can Your Sponge or Loofah Make You Sick
content:
Title:
Can Your Sponge or Loofah Make You Sick?

Keywords:
sponge hygiene, loofah bacteria, skin infections, bathing tools, Nigerian skincare, loofah risks, fungal infections, sponge safety, clean skin habits

Short Description:
Your sponge or loofah could be harming your skin more than helping it. Here's what every woman should know about using them safely.

Can Your Sponge or Loofah Make You Sick?

You step into the bathroom, grab your sponge or loofah, and scrub your body clean. It's part of your daily routine.

But what if I told you that same sponge could be the reason behind your skin rashes, itching, stubborn pimples or even infections?

Yes, the same thing you use to stay clean can actually make you sick, especially if you're not using it the right way or keeping it clean.

Let me show you how this affects you.

Why Sponges and Loofahs Can Be Risky

Your traditional Nigerian bathing sponge (net sponge or "sapalọ" sponge) or loofah might look clean, but underneath, it can be a perfect hiding place for germs.

Here's why:

  • They stay wet for hours after your bath, and bacteria love moisture.
  • They collect dead skin cells, body oils, sweat, and dirt while you bathe. That mixture becomes food for germs.
  • Most people don't rinse or dry them properly, so the bacteria just keep growing.
  • If you hang it inside the bathroom, the damp, humid air makes it worse. Research shows that moist, warm environments (like bathrooms) help bacteria and fungi grow fast on personal hygiene items like loofahs and body sponges.

Some of the common germs found on dirty sponges include:

  • Staphylococcus aureus: Linked to skin infections and boils
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa: A common sponge-dwelling bacterium that thrives in moisture, can worsen body odour, and cause rashes or skin infections.
  • Candida: A fungus that may cause itching and yeast infections in body folds
  • Even mould, if it's never dried out properly

All of these can end up on your skin when you reuse the sponge.

How This Can Affect Your Skin

Using a dirty sponge or loofah isn't just gross; it can cause skin problems. These are some of the common issues:

  • Breakouts: You may notice more pimples on your back, chest, or bum, especially if your sponge is spreading bacteria instead of cleaning them off.
  • Itching or Rashes: If fungi like Candida are growing on your sponge, you could develop itchy patches, especially under your breasts, inner thighs, or between your butt cheeks.
  • Worsened Skin Conditions: For people with eczema or sensitive skin, dirty sponges can trigger flare-ups, redness, or irritation.
  • Infections: Shaving bumps or small cuts can get infected if your sponge carries germs like Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Body Odour or Rashes: If your sponge smells bad or feels slimy, it's likely full of bacteria. Using it will only transfer that smell and irritation to your body.
  • Boils and Folliculitis: Reusing a dirty sponge can clog your pores and cause painful boils or inflamed hair follicles.

Signs Your Sponge Is Unsafe to Use

  • It smells weird: A sour or musty smell means germs are already present.
  • It feels slimy: That slippery feel isn't normal; it's a sign of bacteria or mould buildup.
  • It's discoloured: If the colour is fading or has dark spots, dump it.
  • You've used it for more than 3 to 4 weeks: Even if it looks fine, it's likely full of hidden germs.
  • Your skin reacts after use: If you feel itchy, notice more pimples, or develop a rash after bathing, your sponge may be the culprit.

If any of these sound familiar, it's time to let that sponge go.

How to Use Sponges Safely

If you still prefer using a sponge or loofah, that's fine, just make sure you're using it the safe way:

  • Rinse it well after every bath to remove soap, dirt, and dead skin.
  • Squeeze out all the water before hanging it.
  • Hang it in a well-ventilated area, not in a wet bathroom.
  • Avoid using it on broken skin, cuts, or after shaving.
  • Wash it regularly with hot water or disinfect it once a week.
  • Replace it every 3 to 4 weeks, even if it appears to be fine.
  • Please don't use it on your face or private areas. These are delicate zones.
  • Never share your sponge, not even with your sibling or spouse.

Better Alternatives to Try

If you're tired of dealing with sponges that get dirty too fast, here are safer and more hygienic options you can consider:

  • Silicone scrubbers: They don't hold water, so germs don't grow easily. Plus, they're extremely easy to clean and last longer.
  • Exfoliating gloves: These are good for scrubbing, but make sure you wash and dry them properly after each use.
  • Your hands and a soft towel: Sometimes, less is more. For sensitive or acne-prone skin, your hands can be cleaned with a mild soap without irritation.

Regardless of what you use, the key is to keep it clean and dry after every use.

Final Thoughts

Every woman's skincare journey is unique, but the simple act of bathing should never compromise your skin's health.

If you've ever experienced unexplained breakouts, itching, or bumps after bathing, it may be time to take a closer look at what you're using, not just the soap.

Have you ever had skin issues you think were caused by a sponge or loofah you used in the bath? Or found a method that works better for you?

I'd love to hear what your experience has been. Let's talk about it.
